prompt.context: Our client is a for-profit, specialty college named Chic Cosmetology University (CCU). Founded in 2005, CCU is a program for high school graduates seeking their professional cosmetology license. CCU is currently the market leader for cosmetology education with campuses in ten major metropolitan areas in the US. CCU has capital to invest in a new campus and is considering Chicagoland as a location.
prompt.question: Should CCU open a new campus in the Chicagoland area?

clarifying_info.q: What does success look like for this new campus?
clarifying_info.a: The client considers a successful launch as achieving positive operating profit for the new campus two years after opening.

clarifying_info.q: How long do students attend CCU?
clarifying_info.a: Enrolled students take classes at a physical campus for one school year to earn their degree. The fiscal year begins on September 1.
CCU boasts the best campuses in the industry with state-of-the-art equipment and strong job placement due to CCU's relationships with top salons in local areas.

clarifying_info.q: What is the competitive landscape like?
clarifying_info.a: There are 2-3 other large specialty colleges, some of which are in the same geographies as CCU. Community colleges are also beginning to offer cosmetology degrees at lower prices. All ten CCU campuses and all competitor campuses have been present for at least three full school years.
CCU and industry enrollments are growing at 5% per year. A high school diploma and cosmetology degree are required to enter the field. 98% of cosmetologists are women.

clarifying_info.q: What is the investment required to open a new campus in Chicago?
clarifying_info.a: The total cost is $4.5M in initial building costs to renovate the chosen site. These costs can be amortized evenly over a three-year period. Fixed costs otherwise remain flat per year.

exhibits.title: 2010 CCU Financials
exhibits.shows: A financial summary table for CCU as of 8/31/2010, with figures in thousands of dollars, covering all existing campuses combined.

exhibits.title: CCU and major competitor locations
exhibits.shows: A table listing each CCU campus city with its 2010 market share (share of total potential students as defined by CCU), alongside a map showing CCU campus and major competitor campus locations.

data.note: Share measured as share of total potential students; data as of 8/31/2010

framework: 1. Evaluate CCU revenue and cost structures (revenue per student, fixed costs per campus, variable costs per student, gross profit per student)
2. Determine break-even enrollment for the new Chicago campus, incorporating initial investment amortization
3. Estimate the total addressable market and CCU's projected market share in Chicago
4. Project Year 1 and Year 2 enrollments and assess whether break-even is achievable within two years
5. Identify qualitative factors and strategic alternatives

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the key unit economics for a single CCU campus: average revenue per student, fixed costs per campus, variable cost per student, and gross profit per student.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will quickly derive per-campus and per-student metrics by dividing totals by 10 campuses (or 10,000 students). They should arrive at: revenue per student = $15K, fixed cost per campus = $4.8M, variable cost per student = $8K, gross profit per student = $7K.

math.setup: All figures from Exhibit 1 (in $000s). 10 campuses, 10,000 total enrolled students.
steps: Total annual fixed cost per campus = $48,000K / 10 campuses = $4,800K = $4.8M
Total variable cost per student = $80,000K / 10,000 students = $8K
math.answer: Revenue per student: $15K; Fixed cost per campus: $4.8M; Variable cost per student: $8K; Gross profit per student: $7K

questions.prompt: What is the break-even number of student enrollments required for the Chicago campus in Year 1? (Assume $4.5M initial building cost amortized evenly over 3 years, and flat fixed costs otherwise.)
questions.guidance: Candidate must add the annual amortization charge ($1.5M) to the base fixed cost ($4.8M) to get total annual fixed costs of $6.3M, then divide by gross profit per student to find break-even enrollments of 900.

math.setup: Initial investment = $4.5M; amortization period = 3 years; base fixed cost per campus = $4.8M; gross profit per student = $7K.
math.answer: 900 students per year needed to break even

questions.prompt: What types of schools and students should CCU target in its Chicago marketing strategy?
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover school type (public high schools, middle-class area schools near the campus geographically) and student profile (women high school graduates not attending a 4-year college who are interested in cosmetology). After the candidate identifies several criteria, share that CCU has identified 1,000 targeted high schools in Chicagoland, and that within these schools CCU's market research estimates on average 6 students per school have potential for CCU enrollment.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what market share should CCU project for the Chicago campus in Year 1, and why?
questions.guidance: Candidates should observe: campuses without competitors present tend to achieve ~15% share, while campuses with at least one competitor present tend to achieve ~10% share (Houston 10%). Having more than one competitor does not further reduce share (Boston has 8% with only one competitor, which is anomalous). Chicago will have one competitor, so 10% is the appropriate assumption. Candidates should also note that these shares reflect campuses that have been operating for at least 3 years — an excellent candidate will flag that Year 1/Year 2 share is likely lower than 10%.

questions.prompt: How many students should CCU Chicago expect to enroll at most in Year 1? Can it break even in Year 1?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate total potential students (HS + Adult), apply the 10% market share, and compare to the 900-student break-even threshold. Share the following if not already given: 80% of enrolled students come directly from high school; the other 20% come from the adult market.

math.setup: 1,000 targeted high schools; 6 potential students per HS; 80% of market is HS students (20% adult). Projected market share = 10%. Break-even = 900 students.
steps: Potential HS students = 6 students/HS x 1,000 HS = 6,000 students
HS students represent 80% of total market, so total potential = 6,000 / 0.80 = 7,500 students
Alternatively: Potential adult students = 6,000 x 25% = 1,500 students; total = 6,000 + 1,500 = 7,500 students
Break-even required = 900 students — CCU falls short in both Year 1 and Year 2
math.answer: CCU can expect at most 750 students in Year 1. This is 150 students short of the 900 needed to break even. Year 2 projects ~788 students, still below break-even.

questions.prompt: (Bonus, if time permits) Suppose CCU finds a lot with a one-time construction cost of $300K (same 3-year amortization schedule). Should they enter Chicago now?
questions.guidance: Candidate recalculates break-even with lower amortization ($100K/year instead of $1.5M/year). Break-even drops to 700 students. Year 1 enrollment of 750 exceeds this threshold — but an excellent candidate will flag that the 10% market share benchmark comes from campuses open for 3+ years, so Year 1 share is likely below 10%, making 750 an optimistic ceiling. This makes the decision much closer and merits further analysis.

math.setup: New construction cost = $300K; amortization over 3 years; base fixed cost = $4.8M; gross profit per student = $7K.
math.answer: With a $300K site, break-even is 700 students. Year 1 enrollment projection of 750 nominally exceeds this, but the 10% share assumption may be optimistic for a brand-new campus.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative issues should CCU consider as it evaluates the Chicago market entry decision?

categories.name: Demand-side levers
ideas: Offer scholarships to increase the number of potential students or improve conversion rate among identified prospects
Partner with public high schools in Chicagoland to recruit directly from target student segments
Conduct deeper market research to test whether the 6 potential students per HS assumption holds in Chicago

categories.name: Supply/cost-side levers
ideas: Reduce fixed costs by transporting equipment and materials from existing campuses that are not at full capacity
Negotiate a lower-cost site (e.g., the $300K lot scenario) to reduce the break-even threshold
Pursue a phased opening with smaller initial footprint to lower up-front fixed costs

categories.name: Alternative market strategies
ideas: Evaluate other cities beyond Chicagoland that currently have no CCU presence and potentially higher market share
Add a second campus in a high-share city like New York City or Atlanta where CCU already has strong relationships and brand recognition
Explore the adult (non-HS) market more aggressively, as it represents 20% of potential and may be more addressable in Year 1

categories.name: Competitive risks
ideas: Community colleges offering cosmetology at lower prices could erode CCU's premium positioning
A new competitor could enter Chicago after CCU opens, further reducing market share below 10%
The 10% share benchmark reflects mature campuses (3+ years); Year 1 share could be materially lower

recommendation: CCU should NOT open a Chicago campus under the current cost structure. At the projected 10% market share, Year 1 enrollment would reach only 750 students — 150 short of the 900-student break-even threshold. Year 2 enrollment of ~788 students also falls short, meaning the campus would not achieve the client's target of positive operating profit within two years.
risks: The 10% market share assumption may be too optimistic for a new campus: Exhibit 2 data reflects campuses that have been operating for at least 3 years, so Year 1 share is likely below 10%
Community college competition at lower price points could suppress CCU's enrollment further
If Chicago has only one competitor, there is a risk of a second entrant after CCU opens, further diluting share
next_steps: Explore the $300K site option: break-even drops to 700 students, which Year 1 enrollments could nominally reach — but validate whether Year 1 share will actually hit 10%
Conduct market research in other Chicagoland high schools to test the 6-students-per-HS assumption and identify higher-potential clusters
Evaluate alternative cities with no CCU presence and higher market potential per targeted high school
Consider scholarships or direct school partnerships to improve conversion and reduce the effective break-even threshold
